Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The study is centered on designing and evaluating input solutions (micro light switch, flexible sensors, EMG, etc.) to enable communication and environmental control for a child with SMA. The primary focus is utilitarian: identifying appropriate input devices for communication, power wheelchair, and environmental control. A custom interactive game using a favorite character (minions) is created later as an engaging task to evaluate these input solutions, indicating fun is incorporated after the utilitarian mechanics are defined. This aligns with a mostly utility-first design rather than fun-first or equal fun-utility.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely symmetrical (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) mostly symmetrical (i.e., undertale's differing NPC behaviors based on previous playthroughs),
        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),
        (4) mostly asymmetrical (i.e., tag),
        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: The study is a single-participant case evaluating input devices for a child with severe motor impairments using an interactive game tailored specifically to him. There is no indication of multiple players with shared or mirrored roles; instead, the system and the child have fundamentally different capabilities and roles (system presents stimuli, child provides limited input via specialized sensors). This aligns best with an entirely asymmetrical interaction structure, similar in spirit to assistive or trainer–trainee setups rather than symmetric multiplayer games.
